title: Smallest Word Through a Stack
statement:
You get a lowercase string s, an empty holding stack t, and an empty output string. You may repeat either move, in any order, until s and t are both empty:

  • Take the first character of s and push it on top of t.
  • Pop the top character of t and append it to the output.

Return the alphabetically smallest output you can produce.

examples.why: Push c, push a, pop a. Push b, then pop b and c.
The a comes last, so everything must be pushed first. After a, the stack pops c before b: "abcd" is impossible.
Pop the first b even though another b is still to come. Popping only when the top is strictly smaller than everything left gives "bcbc".

constraints: s has only lowercase English letters
hints: The output grows from the front, so you want the smallest letter you can get next, as early as possible. When should you pop the top of the stack?
Pop the top whenever it is no larger than every letter still in s. Otherwise, some smaller letter is still coming, so keep pushing.
Precompute the minimum letter of every suffix of s, so the check "is the top ≤ everything left" is O(1).

explain.intuition:
At any moment you can either output the stack's top now, or keep pushing to reach letters further on in s. If some letter still in s is smaller than the top, waiting is better: you can push up to it and output it first. If no remaining letter is smaller, the top is the best letter you could ever output next, so pop it now.

Equal letters must also pop. Holding back a b to wait for another b gains nothing and may trap the first b under bigger letters, as "cbcb" shows. A suffix-minimum array makes the test O(1), so the whole thing is linear, the same way a monotonic stack decides when to pop.
steps: Build sufMin[i] = the smallest letter in s[i..], with a sentinel larger than z at index n.
For each index i, push s[i] onto the stack.
Then, while the stack is non-empty and its top ≤ sufMin[i + 1], pop it into the output.
Return the output. The sentinel guarantees the stack is empty at the end.
pitfalls: Popping only when the top is strictly smaller than the rest. Ties must pop, see "cbcb".
Comparing the top with the next character of s instead of the minimum of everything left.
Recomputing the minimum of the rest each time, which makes it O(n²) on long inputs.

solutions.title: Rescan the remaining letters
solutions.idea: Same greedy rule, but find the smallest remaining letter by scanning the rest of s every time.

solutions.title: Stack with suffix minimums
solutions.idea: Pop while the top is no larger than the smallest letter still waiting in s, which a suffix-minimum array gives in O(1).

followups: Replace the suffix-minimum array with 26 letter counts. How do you find the smallest remaining letter quickly?
Prove that popping on ties is never worse than waiting.
lcTitle: Using a Robot to Print the Lexicographically Smallest String
